title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Open research intelligence for academic research organizations Every contribution, connected. Tessera builds your organization's research footprint from public data: people, publications, grants, and clinical studies, linked with the evidence behind every connection. Curators confirm links in seconds, and everyone can find who works on what, who should meet, what followed the work, and which funding fits it next. Get started Try the demo Source on GitHub Starts from public data PubMed, NIH RePORTER, ClinicalTrials.gov, iCite, ORCID, MeSH, and Grants.gov. No HR feeds or integrations to begin. title: Overview
heading: See why, every time
text: Every suggested link between a person and a paper comes with its evidence, weighed in plain language: the ORCID iD on the paper, the organization in the affiliation, a grant it acknowledges, shared coauthors, a different first name. Weights can be learned from your own decisions, and auto-accept switches on only where the measured precision allows. How suggestions are scored → Fast curation

title: Overview
heading: Curate in minutes, not months
text: The review queue puts strong matches first, grouped by person, with the matched author and their affiliation highlighted. Accept, reject, or defer from the keyboard; accept all of a person's strong matches in one step, and undo anything. The review queue → Expertise

title: Overview
heading: Who works on what
text: Ask in plain words, such as "memory T cells". Tessera reads the question through your organization's papers, shows the concepts it understood, and ranks people by what they actually publish, with the matching concepts on every result. Finding experts → Connections

title: Overview
heading: See the shape of your organization
text: Who works with whom, and how research areas connect. Groups are found from the network itself and named by what they work on; people who bridge groups are marked. Every graph has a list view with the same information. Connections → Collaboration

title: Overview
heading: Who should meet
text: Missed connections are people whose interests are alike but who have never worked together, with the topics they share and anyone who has worked with both. The unit matrix shows which units share interests but rarely collaborate. Missed connections → Groups

title: Overview
heading: A home for every lab and program
text: Divisions, programs, labs, and shared resources each get a page: their leaders and people, alumni, the papers that are theirs, their grants, studies, themes, and openings. Their own managers arrange it from approved blocks and publish it, with drafts, history, and rollback, and a weekly inbox brings them what changed. Groups → Portfolio

title: Overview
heading: The portfolio, honestly
text: Publications, funding, topics, and studies for the organization, a division, a program, a lab, or people you pick, over the years you choose. Every figure says exactly what it counts, with its definition and version, its cohort, and its sources; money is counted without double counting, small numbers are marked, and nothing ranks people. Freeze a report as a snapshot that verifies years later, and export any figure with the records behind it. Insight → Impact

title: Overview
heading: What followed the work
text: Every grant shows what came after it: the papers that acknowledge it, the registered studies that reference them, and the clinical articles that cite them, with practice guidelines marked and the years from award to first clinical citation. Each step says how it is linked and where that came from, and only confirmed links are followed. It shows association, never causation. A grant's thread → Funding

title: Overview
heading: Funding that fits
text: Federal opportunities from Grants.gov, and your own foundation calls, pilot funds, and limited submissions, each read as topics and matched to the people and groups whose confirmed work fits it, with the reasons shown. Whether your organization may apply is checked separately: applicant type, deadlines, limited submission, career stage. Start a team from an opportunity to see which topics its members cover, who could fill the gaps, and a brief to share. Opportunities → Optional assistant

title: Overview
heading: Ask, and see the sources
text: Turn on the assistant and ask in plain words: who works on this, what followed that grant, which opportunities fit this lab. It looks things up with read-only tools, as the person asking, so it sees only what they may see, and every answer cites the records it rests on. A citation it cannot stand behind is removed, and a question the records do not answer is declined, never guessed. It works with any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic-compatible endpoint, official, self-hosted, or a model on your own machine, and with Amazon Bedrock. It is off until you turn it on, and every exchange is logged. The assistant → Plain language

title: Overview
heading: Summaries people approve
text: With the assistant on, a profile or a group can have a short summary of its work for patients, donors, and students, drafted from confirmed records only. Nobody sees a draft but its reviewers: the person, their curators, or the group's managers, who edit, approve, or reject it. Approved summaries are labeled as drafted with AI assistance, and by whom they were approved. Plain-language summaries → Public

title: Overview
heading: A public site, checked
text: Groups and people who opt in get plain, fast public pages in your colors: citations and links, never abstracts, and nothing that is not on an allowlist. Every build is checked for accessibility, broken links, and color contrast before it replaces the last. The public site →

title: Overview
heading: How it works
text: Connectors fetch public records into a Parquet lake. The evidence engine builds the directory and suggests links, each with its evidence; curators decide in the ledger; and the search index and discovery data feed a JSON API and a fast, accessible web app.

title: Overview
heading: Try it in a minute
text: Tessera needs uv , which provides Python 3.12 or newer. The demo builds an invented research institute, with about 100 people, their publications, grants, studies, and a curator's decisions: git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/tessera.git cd tessera uv sync uv run tessera demo uv run tessera --config demo/tessera.toml serve Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 . title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Getting started This guide takes you from a fresh checkout to a running Tessera with your organization's public research footprint: people, publications, grants, and clinical studies, connected with evidence. It takes about 15 minutes of your time; the first sync then runs on its own for a few minutes to an hour, depending on the size of the organization.

title: Getting started
heading: What you need
text: A Mac, Linux, or Windows machine (a laptop is fine) with internet access to the public sources: NCBI (PubMed and iCite), NIH RePORTER, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ORCID. uv , which installs the right Python (3.12 or newer) and Tessera's dependencies for you. Disk space: about 100 MB for a mid-sized research institute (a few thousand papers over five years), and a few gigabytes for a large academic medical center. Everything lives in one folder, the data home . Tessera needs no institutional systems, accounts, or credentials. An NCBI API key is optional and makes PubMed requests faster (see Configuration ).

title: Getting started
heading: Install
text: git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/tessera.git cd tessera uv sync Then create a configuration file and a data home: uv run tessera init This writes tessera.toml in the current folder and creates ./var for data. Run uv run tessera doctor at any time to check the installation.

title: Getting started
heading: Try the demo first (optional)
text: To see Tessera working before you describe your own organization, build the demo, an invented research institute with about 100 people, their publications, grants, and studies, and a curator's decisions: uv run tessera demo # builds ./demo in a few seconds uv run tessera --config demo/tessera.toml serve Everyone and everything in it is invented. Delete the demo folder when you are done; it is separate from your own installation. It runs without sign-in; add --port 9000 (or another port) to serve if 8000 is taken. The demo is built with the optional assistant off. Trying it on the demo shows the few lines that turn it on there.

title: Getting started
heading: Describe your organization
text: Tessera finds your organization in public records by name, so the [organization] section of tessera.toml matters more than anything else. title: Getting started

Searches PubMed for each person by name, then fetches citation metrics from iCite and the public ORCID records of people whose ORCID iD it knows. Scores every candidate paper for every person and records suggestions with their evidence, along with links between papers, grants, and studies. title: Describing your organization
heading: Describing your organization
text: Describing your organization Tessera has no HR feed. It recognizes your organization in public records by how the organization's name is written there: in author affiliations on papers, on NIH grants, and in clinical trial registrations. The [organization] section of tessera.toml is that description, and it decides what Tessera finds. A good profile finds nearly everything that belongs to you and very little that does not. This guide explains each setting, how to find the right values, and how to check the result.

Search NIH RePORTER for a project you know is yours and copy the organization name exactly as it appears under Organization . title: Curating
heading: Curating
text: Curating Tessera suggests; people decide. Every link between a person and a paper starts as a suggestion with a likelihood and the evidence behind it. Curators confirm or reject suggestions, and those decisions are permanent: later syncs add evidence but never change a decision. This guide covers the review queue, discovered people, and the tools around them.

title: Curating
heading: How suggestions are scored
text: For each person, Tessera looks at every paper with a compatible author name and adds up evidence for and against a match. Each item of evidence carries a weight and a plain-language explanation, for example: For: the author's ORCID iD matches the person's; the paper is listed on the person's public ORCID record; the same ORCID iD appears on the person's other papers; an email at your domain; your organization in the affiliation; the paper acknowledges the person's grant; coauthors who also appear on the person's other papers; the full first name matches; the paper's topics fit the person's work; a journal they publish in. Against: a different ORCID iD, or one you marked as not theirs; a diff

heading: The review queue
text: Open Review queue in the sidebar. Suggestions are listed on the left in priority order: strong matches first, grouped by person so they can be confirmed quickly, then possible matches with conflicting evidence, then ambiguous names. The panel on the right shows the selected suggestion: the paper, the author list with the matched position highlighted and its affiliation on that paper, the likelihood, each item of evidence with its weight, and the history of decisions. heading: Possible duplicates
text: The same person sometimes has two records, typically one from a roster and one from grant records, when the roster row shares no identifier with the grant record. A name alone never proposes a pair. Merge into… moves the left record's papers, grants, units, names, and identifiers to the record on the right, which is kept. Keep … instead merges the other way. title: Curating
heading: ORCID iDs
text: An ORCID iD is the strongest evidence Tessera has: a researcher's own identifier, printed on many papers. When an iD appears at a person's author position on at least two of their likely papers, Tessera suggests it on their profile, under Identifiers , with how many of their papers carry it and, once it has been read, what the public ORCID record says. Tessera never confirms an iD on its own. Confirm makes the iD the person's. From the next sync, papers carrying it match decisively, papers listed on the person's ORCID record count as strong evidence (and are fetched from PubMed if Tessera lacks them), and papers carrying a different iD count against. title: Curating
heading: Learned weights and auto-accept
text: Admin → Evidence shows how suggestions are scored and how well, measured on your own decisions. Curators can look; admins can change it. Evaluate now fits learned weights to your accept and reject decisions and compares them with the hand-set ones on people left out of the fit. Once there are enough decisions (200, with 20 rejections, about 5 people) and the learned model predicts better, Release it makes it active from the next sync; Use hand-set weights goes back. Auto-accept can be switched on only at a score where the evaluation measured at least 99% precision over at least 50 decisions. Each sync then accepts open suggestions at or above it that have no conflicting evidence. They are ma

title: Curating
heading: The decision log
text: Decision log lists every decision across the organization, newest first: what was decided, about which person and record, by whom, when, and with what note. Link decisions open their evidence, where the latest decision can be undone. Decisions are never deleted. Undo is itself a recorded decision that restores the previous state, so the log always shows the full story.

title: Curating
heading: What survives a sync
text: A decision locks the link: later syncs and rescoring never change an accepted or rejected status. If a source stops reporting a link (a grant drops a paper, for instance), the link is marked as no longer reported rather than deleted. Dismissed people stay dismissed; promoted people stay members. Search and lists reflect decisions on the next request. Topic summaries on profiles refresh at the next sync.

title: Curating
heading: Who decides
text: With accounts on, every decision is recorded under the name of the person who signed in, and each person decides only what their role allows: curators for everyone or for one unit or person, researchers for the suggestions about themselves (their queue is My suggestions ). Without accounts (single-operator mode, on this machine only), every decision is recorded under the [server] operator name. See Accounts and sign-in .

title: Finding experts
heading: Finding experts
text: Finding experts Tessera describes each person's research with the MeSH headings that PubMed indexers attach to their papers. From those it answers "who works on this?", lists people with similar interests on every profile, draws who works with whom, and shows exactly what drives each person's topics. This guide explains what you see and how it is built.

title: Finding experts
heading: Who works on…?
text: Open Find experts in the sidebar (or press / and type "experts") and describe a topic in your own words: a disease, a method, a cell type, a question. Tessera reads your words through the papers they find. It searches the organization's papers, gathers the MeSH headings those papers share, and turns them into a small set of concepts. They are shown above the results as Understood as : Select × on a concept to drop it, if the search drifted somewhere you did not mean. Type in Add a concept to choose a heading by name, for example "Neoplasms", and add it. Select a concept on any result, or on a profile, to start a new search from that concept alone. People are ranked by how well their topics m

title: Finding experts
heading: Topics on a profile
text: Each profile's Topics card lists the person's most distinctive concepts. How this is built opens the full list, with, for each concept: its weight, relative to their strongest concept; how many of their papers carry it, and how many of those are confirmed; from keywords , when the concept comes only from authors' keywords on papers that have no MeSH headings yet. Above the topics, research areas show where they fall in MeSH's hierarchy: the diseases, body systems, organisms, and processes the person studies, such as "Neoplasms 34%" or "Nervous System 21%". Areas that nearly everyone in the organization shares count for less, as topics do; molecules and methods stay topics rather than areas.

title: Finding experts
heading: Similar people
text: The Similar people card on a profile lists the people whose topics overlap most, with the concepts they share. Pairs are worked out when profiles are built, not when you look, so the list is instant. Similarity reflects the topics of people's papers. It says nothing about the quality of anyone's work or whether they are available to collaborate.

title: Finding experts
heading: Connections
text: Connections , in the sidebar, draws three pictures of the organization and lists two kinds of opportunity. Each picture has a List view with the same people, topics, and relationships as sortable tables, for keyboard and screen-reader use, or for copying. View Shows Use it to see Collaboration People. A solid line means they share papers, grants, or studies; it is thicker the more they share and the fewer others share it. A dashed line means similar interests without any shared work Who works together, and who might Person focus One person, their top topics, and the people who share those topics, gathered around them Who shares someone's interests, and around what Concept landscape Topics, l

title: Finding experts
heading: Missed connections
text: Missed connections lists pairs of current members whose interests are alike but who have never published, held a grant, or run a study together, most alike first. Each pair shows the topics they share, and, when someone has worked with both, that person, who might introduce them. Limit the list to one unit, or to pairs in different units, and choose how alike they must be. Missed connections

title: Finding experts
heading: Units
text: Units compares every pair of units (the 30 largest with at least two members, by default). In each cell, the shade shows how alike the two units' members are, and the inner square how much they work together, both per possible pair of people, so large and small units compare fairly. A strong shade with a small square marks units that share interests but rarely work together. Select a cell, or move with the arrow keys and press Enter, to see the people behind it, with what they share and whether they have worked together. The List view has every pair of units as a sortable table. Units

title: Finding experts
heading: Saved searches
text: Any search can be saved: Save search on the People, Publications, Grants, or Studies page keeps the words and filters, and on Search it keeps a search of everything. What the search finds when you save it counts as seen. A saved search with new matches Your saved searches are listed on the home page with how many matches are new since you last looked. Opening one shows the new matches above the results; Mark as seen clears them. Saved searches are your own: nobody else sees them. Up to 5,000 matches are remembered for each; a search that finds more still shows its count.

title: Finding experts
heading: Keeping it current
text: tessera sync rebuilds profiles, similar people, and the graphs at the end of every run. To rebuild them alone, for example after many curation decisions or a change to [discovery] : tessera build discovery Until profiles have been built once, Find experts says so instead of showing results.

title: Groups
heading: Groups
text: Groups Groups are how your organization is arranged: divisions, departments, programs, centers, shared resources, labs, and any other kind you name. Each group has people, with their roles and the dates they joined and left. A group can sit under several others; for example, a program can span two divisions. You can curate groups by hand in the app, through the API, or from a file. Each group and membership records where it came from and the identifier it has there, so an export from your HR or organization system can supply groups later without creating duplicates.

title: Groups
heading: Kinds, roles, and what you call them
text: The [vocabulary] section of the configuration names the kinds of group you offer, the roles people hold in them, and what the app calls a group: [vocabulary] group = "Group" groups = "Groups" leader_roles = ["lead", "co_lead"] # listed as a group's leaders default_role = "member" # for memberships that name no role attributable_kinds = ["program", "lab"] # kinds whose papers are suggested as their own [vocabulary.kinds] division = "Division" program = "Program" lab = "Lab" [vocabulary.roles] lead = "Lead" member = "Member" trainee = "Trainee" Groups and memberships store the key ( lab , trainee ), and the app shows the label . title: Groups
heading: Themes and projects
text: A group can describe what it works on in its own words: themes (long-lived questions) and projects (pieces of work with an end). An opening leaves the page by itself after its closing date, so nobody has to remember to take it down. Close now takes it down early; changing its date extends it.

text: Admin → Groups lists every group with its kind, the groups it sits within, its current members and alumni, and where it came from. Filter by kind or find a group by name or code. Archived groups are hidden unless you ask for them. Open a group to see its members. Current lists the people who belong now, leaders first; Alumni lists the people whose memberships have ended. From a group's page you can: Add member: find a person in the directory, then choose their role, an optional title, and the dates. title: Groups
heading: Importing groups from a file
text: uv run tessera groups import groups.csv --source hr uv run tessera groups import memberships.csv --source hr --source names where the file comes from. It can be any short name, such as hr or registry , but use the same name every time, because each row's identifier is unique only within its source. Importing the same source again updates the groups and memberships it made earlier.

title: Groups
heading: What an import changes
text: The source is in charge of what it supplies. An import overwrites the fields its rows give, and replaces the parent links it made earlier. Links you added by hand stay. A row without an identifier matches a group by code, then by name. A group made by hand is adopted by the first import whose row matches it and carries an identifier: from then on it belongs to that source. A group merged by hand is still found: an import that names a merged group's identifier updates the group it was merged into. A membership you removed stays removed. --complete says the file is the source's whole list. Groups from this source that the file no longer lists are archived, and current memberships from this sou

title: Groups
heading: The roster is one way in
text: The roster import ( tessera people import ) adds people, and the groups and memberships on its rows. A roster row can now give a group's kind ( kind ) and the person's role ( role ) as well as the group's name and code. Groups and memberships from the roster are recorded as coming from roster , so importing the roster again updates them.

title: Groups
heading: Through the API
text: Admins can do all of this through the API: POST /api/v1/groups creates a group, POST /api/v1/groups/{group} changes, nests, archives, or restores one, POST /api/v1/groups/{group}/merge merges it, and /api/v1/groups/{group}/members adds, changes, ends, and removes memberships. POST /api/v1/groups/import?source=hr takes the same rows as the JSON file, with complete and dry_run , so a scheduled job can feed groups from another system. Anyone signed in can read groups, members, and history. See The API .

title: Groups
heading: Curator scopes
text: A curator can be limited to the people of one group (Admin → Accounts). The scope includes every group beneath it, through any of its parents, and only people whose memberships are current.

title: Groups
heading: Showing a group on its own website
text: A public group's publications, people, openings, and news can be embedded in its own website, and kept current by every publication of the public site: see Embedding group content . Managers find the code in Edit page → Embed on another website .

title: Insight
heading: Insight
text: Insight Insight shows what the organization, a division, a program, or a lab publishes, is funded for, and runs as studies, over the years you choose. It is built for people who have to stand behind a number. Every figure says exactly what it counts, for whom, over which years, and from which sources, and the records behind it are one click away. Open it from Insight → Portfolio in the menu. The portfolio overview

title: Insight
heading: Reading a figure
text: Every figure is a metric over a cohort and a period : the metric says what is counted, and how (see Definitions ); the cohort says whose work counts (see Cohorts ); the period is a span of years: calendar years for papers and studies, and the funder's fiscal years for grants. Under each figure, one line names the cohort and its size, the period, when each source was last fetched, and the metric with its version, such as publications.count/v1 . About opens the full account: What it shows and What is counted : the metric's definition and its counting rule, word for word; For whom, and when : the cohort with its size and how its members' work is counted, the period, and the options chosen; Sour

title: Insight
heading: Confirmed and likely
text: A paper counts for a member when their authorship is confirmed , or when it is a strong suggestion nobody has decided yet: the same papers that count on profiles. Rejected and weaker suggestions never count. Figures show the two apart (confirmed in solid, likely in a lighter shade) and the notes say how many are likely. Choose Confirmed only in the bar at the top to count decided papers alone.

title: Insight
heading: Small numbers
text: Counts from 1 to 4 are small numbers : one paper more or less changes them a lot, and they may point at a handful of people. They are hatched in charts and marked † in tables, and trends are never claimed from them. Set the threshold with [insight] small_number (see Configuration ).

title: Insight
heading: Incomplete years
text: The first sync collects a set number of years of history ( [sync] window_years , five by default). Years before that are incomplete: a figure that reaches back past them dims them and says so, and the period starts at the first complete year unless you choose otherwise.

title: Insight
heading: No league tables
text: No figure ranks people. Figures break down by year, funder, activity, topic, phase, or group. Where a table lists groups, it is in alphabetical order until you sort it.

title: Insight
heading: Cohorts
text: The Cohort button at the top of every Insight page chooses whose work is counted: Cohort Who Written in the address as The organization Everyone in the directory, current and former organization (the default) A group Its members; with Include the groups beneath it , theirs too group:<address> , group:<address>+below Picked people The people listed people:<ID>,<ID> A search The people a directory search finds search:<words> A saved cohort Any of the above, under a name its ID, coh_… For a group, While members (the default) counts each member's work from the year they joined to the year they left, where the membership's dates are known; a member with no dates counts throughout. title: Insight
heading: Definitions
text: Insight → Definitions lists every metric with its identifier and version, definition, counting rule, unit, years, sources, options, and caveats. A metric's definition never changes in place: counting something differently makes a new version, so a saved report always says what it counted.

text: Figure Metric Shows Publications by year publications.count/v1 The cohort's papers in each year, confirmed and likely Field-normalized citation publications.influence/v1 How the cohort's papers are cited against papers in their own field and year: the distribution of iCite's relative citation ratio Each paper counts once, however many members wrote it (distinct PubMed IDs), in its year of publication. Retracted papers are not counted. PubMed covers biomedical journals; papers in venues it does not index are missing. title: Insight
heading: Topics
text: Topics and their trends Insight → Topics shows what the cohort's papers are about, from the major MeSH headings NLM's indexers give each paper (the headings PubMed marks as a paper's main subjects). Topics ( topics.landscape/v1 ): the cohort's 30 largest topics in the period, each with its papers, its share of the cohort's papers, and its trend. Topics by year ( topics.by_year/v1 ): the 12 largest, with their papers in each year. Topics as: Research areas rolls headings up to the tops of the MeSH branches that name what people study (diseases, anatomy, organisms, psychology, and processes), so that "Breast Neoplasms" and "Melanoma" both count toward Neoplasms; a paper counts once per area. title: Insight
heading: Trends
text: A trend compares a topic's share of the cohort's papers in the later half of the period's complete years with the earlier half (at most three years each; the year under way is left out, because it is not over). A topic is rising when its share grew by a quarter or more, falling when it shrank by a fifth or more, and steady otherwise, but only when the topic has at least small_number papers in each half. Otherwise it says too few papers to tell , and with fewer than four complete years in the period, too few years to tell . The notes name the years compared.

title: Insight
heading: Studies
text: The study portfolio Insight → Studies shows clinical studies registered at ClinicalTrials.gov that were under way at some time in the period: started by its end and not completed before it began, by the dates in the registry record. The organization's studies are every study registered under its names, with its members' studies; another cohort's are the studies a member is an official of (confirmed or, unless confirmed only is chosen, a strong suggestion). Figure Metric Shows Studies by registry status studies.by_status/v1 Not yet recruiting, recruiting, active, completed, terminated, and so on Studies by phase studies.by_phase/v1 Early phase 1 to phase 4, combined phases such as phase 1/2,

title: Insight
heading: Impact
text: Insight → Impact shows what followed the cohort's papers. It is association, not causation: a figure says what cites or lists the papers, never that they caused it. title: Insight
heading: A grant's thread
text: Every grant's page ends with What followed this grant : the papers that acknowledge it (from NIH RePORTER's link table or the paper's own PubMed grant list), the registered studies that reference those papers or name the grant, and the clinical articles that cite the papers. Choose a paper, a study, or a clinical article to see only what it is linked to; Paths to practice guidelines shows the papers and studies that lead to a guideline. Only links that are accepted and still reported by their source are followed, so a link a curator rejected never appears. A paper's page lists the clinical articles citing it, and a person's Impact tab lists what followed each of their grants and their confir

title: Insight
heading: Funding
text: The funding portfolio Insight → Funding shows awards from NIH RePORTER (NIH and the other agencies that report to it), counted the way a sponsored-research office counts them, so that nothing is counted twice: Money comes from fiscal-year records. Each record is one award action (a new award, a renewal, a continuing year, or a supplement) and counts once, in its fiscal year. Fiscal years are the funder's: FY2026 ran from October 2025 to September 2026. Subprojects are left out. The components of multi-project awards (the projects and cores of a P01, P30, or U54) report records of their own, but the parent award's record already includes their money. A grant counts once for a cohort, however

title: Insight
heading: Reports and snapshots
text: A report is a named set of figures over one cohort and one period, for everyone who reads Insight. Save as report on any Insight page saves the figures on that page with the cohort, the years, and the options you chose; Insight → Reports lists them. Opening a report computes its figures from the data as it is now, so a report is a question you can ask again. A snapshot freezes a report. Take snapshot on a report (or tessera report snapshot <name> ) computes every figure once and keeps, in snapshots/<id>/ in the data home: the inputs : every table the figures were computed from, for the cohort's people only (its members with their years, their links, and the rows read from PubMed, RePORTER, C

title: Insight
heading: Exports
text: Every figure has Export : CSV, Parquet, or JSON. An export carries its meaning with it: the figure's rows, and the records it counted with the links (and their identifiers) behind each; about.json and README.txt : the metric's definition, version, and counting rule, the cohort with its definition and size, the period, the options and the filters exactly as written in the address, the sources with their data timestamps, the notes, and when it was computed and exported. CSV and Parquet come as a zip ( funding-awarded.csv , funding-awarded-records.csv , about.json , README.txt ); each Parquet file also carries the account in its schema metadata under tessera , so it travels with the data. title: Insight
heading: The API
text: Every figure is at GET /api/v1/insight/figures/<metric> with cohort , start , end , and the metric's options (such as basis=confirmed ); records=true adds the records counted, and /export?format=csv (or parquet , json ) downloads it. GET /api/v1/insight/metrics lists the definitions, /api/v1/insight/cohorts saves and lists cohorts, /api/v1/insight/reports saves and lists reports and takes their snapshots, and /api/v1/insight/snapshots/<id> shows, verifies, and exports a snapshot. See The API .

title: Opportunities
heading: Opportunities
text: Opportunities Opportunities lists funding the organization's people could apply for: forecast and posted federal opportunities from Grants.gov, and the foundation calls, internal pilot funds, and limited submissions the organization tracks itself. For each one, Tessera shows two things, always apart: Who fits : the people and groups whose work matches what the opportunity is about, and why. Whether the organization may apply : its eligibility, check by check, with what each check was decided from. A strong fit says nothing about eligibility, and an opportunity the organization cannot apply for still shows who fits it, because a collaborator elsewhere might.

title: Opportunities
heading: The list
text: Opportunities Open and forecast opportunities come first, the soonest deadline first. Filter by: Status : open, forecast, closed, or archived. Eligibility : meets, check the notice, or does not meet. Closes within 30 or 90 days. From Grants.gov, or tracked here; Kind (federal, foundation, internal, and so on); Sponsor ; NIH activity code ; Category . Fits my work , once your account is linked to your profile: only the opportunities that fit your confirmed work. Search finds opportunities by title, sponsor, number, and description, here and in the search box at the top of every page. Save a search to see new matches as they arrive.

title: Opportunities
heading: An opportunity's page
text: The page shows what the opportunity is about, its dates and money (a forecast's are the sponsor's estimates), and its details: for NIH notices, the activity codes, the clinical-trial rule, and a link to the notice in the NIH Guide.

title: Opportunities
heading: Who fits
text: An opportunity Tessera reads an opportunity as topics, the way an expert search reads a question: the MeSH headings its title and description name (and their synonyms), and the headings of the organization's papers on the same subject. People whose confirmed work matches those topics are listed with the headings that match and how many of their papers carry each. Groups fit through their current members: as well as their best-fitting members do, who are named. Fit comes in two bands, strong and some , and is never a number to rank people by. If the reading is off, remove a topic or add one, and the opportunity is read again; Reset goes back to Tessera's reading.

title: Opportunities
heading: Watch or dismiss
text: Watch puts an opportunity on your home page; Dismiss takes it off your own lists. Neither changes what anyone else sees.

title: Opportunities
heading: Building a team
text: A team Start a team on an opportunity's page makes a team that needs the topics the opportunity was read as; Teams in the menu lists yours, and Start a team there makes one for topics you choose. On a team's page: Coverage shows each topic the team needs against each member: a mark where the topic, or a narrower one, is a prominent part of the topics of their confirmed work (hover it for the heading and its papers). It says what their papers are about, not what they could do. Missing topics lists the topics nobody on the team covers, each with people who do, ordered by how well they cover that gap and shown with their reasons. Add one with a click. Others who fit the opportunity lists the re

title: Opportunities
heading: Where else opportunities appear
text: Home : opportunities that fit your work, and those you watch. A person's profile : the open opportunities that fit them. A group's page : the open opportunities that fit it through its members (inside the organization only, never on the public site). A group's inbox and the weekly digest: opportunities that arrived since the inbox was last reviewed and fit the group.

title: Opportunities
heading: Opportunities the organization tracks
text: Curators for everyone and admins keep these in Admin → Opportunities : add one, edit it, archive it (it is kept, and can be restored), or import many from a spreadsheet. An import is CSV with a header row, or JSON, with these columns: Column Meaning source Who offers or lists it, such as a foundation or the organization's research office (required, or give --source for every row) external_id Its identifier there; importing the same rows again updates them (without one, the number or else the title stands in) kind foundation , internal , federal , state , industry , or other title Required number , sponsor , description , url , eligibility_notes Text posted_on , closes_on , internal_deadline

title: Opportunities
heading: Keeping them current
text: Each tessera sync reads Grants.gov (see Configuration to narrow it by funding category or agency) and then works out who fits each open opportunity, after the concept profiles. The first sync reads every opportunity's details, about one a second (some 1,500 opportunities); later ones read only what changed. tessera build opportunities works out the fits again on its own.

title: The public site
heading: The public site
text: The public site Tessera's app is for your own people, behind your sign-in. tessera publish writes a separate public site : plain pages for the groups and people who opt in, which any web server can serve. The app itself never needs to face the internet. uv run tessera publish The site is written to public/ in the data home, or wherever [publish] out says. It has: a home page with every published group, by kind; a page for every group that opted in, following its published blocks (see Groups ): what it does, its leaders and people, its publications, grants, studies, themes and projects, openings, news, topics, and contact; a page for every person who opted in: their groups and roles, ORCID iD

title: The public site
heading: Who appears
text: Nobody appears unless they opt in. A group opts in with Public page in its page editor (its managers or curators), or tessera groups public <address> . A person opts in with Public profile on their profile (they themselves, if their account is linked to it, or a curator), or tessera people public <ID> . --off on either command takes pages away at the next publication. A group's page lists its people by name and role; only people who opted in link to a profile.

title: The public site
heading: What the site shows, and what it never shows
text: The site is built from an allowlist : every field on it is chosen by name, so nothing new reaches it by accident. Shown Never shown Names, roles, titles, and dates of membership Email addresses of people (a group's own contact address is shown) Confirmed publications, as citations: authors, title, journal, year, with links to the DOI and PubMed Abstracts, suggestions, scores, evidence, and decisions Grants by title, number, institute, and years; studies by title, NCT number, phase, and status Anything from the internal app: IDs, accounts, history, the review queue Topics and research areas, with credit to MeSH Unconfirmed papers: only papers someone confirmed are published A group's themes,

title: The public site
heading: Checked before it is published
text: The site is built in a fresh folder and checked before it replaces the published one. Every page must declare its language, have one title and one main heading with headings in order, have its landmarks (header, labelled navigation, main content, footer), give every link and image a text alternative, carry no scripts (other than structured data), no inline styles, and no event handlers, and link only to pages that exist. The site's colors must meet WCAG 2.2 level AA in both light and dark mode. If anything fails, the command lists the problems, exits with status 1, and leaves the published site as it was. tessera publish --check builds and checks without writing anything. title: The public site
heading: Keeping it current
text: Openings close on their dates and decisions change what is shown, so publish every day after the sync: 30 3 * * * cd /srv/tessera && /usr/local/bin/uv run tessera --quiet publish Serve the output folder with any web server (nginx, Apache, Caddy, or a static host). Pages link to each other with relative addresses ending in index.html , so the site also works from a sub-folder and from disk. Point the server's not-found page at 404.html .

title: Configuration
heading: Configuration
text: Configuration Tessera reads one file, tessera.toml . uv run tessera init writes a commented starting point; the same file is in the repository as tessera.example.toml . Every setting has a sensible default except the organization profile. Tessera checks the whole file when it starts and reports every problem at once, with the setting's name, so a typo never fails silently. Unknown sections and settings are errors too.

title: Configuration
heading: Where the file is
text: Commands look for the configuration in this order: --config PATH (or -c PATH ) on the command line; the TESSERA_CONFIG environment variable; tessera.toml in the current folder. Relative paths inside the file (the data home, logo files) are relative to the file's own folder.

title: Configuration
heading: Environment variables
text: A simple setting can be overridden by an environment variable named TESSERA_<SECTION>_<SETTING> , which is handy for containers and services: TESSERA_SERVER_PORT=9000 uv run tessera serve TESSERA_DATA_HOME=/srv/tessera/data uv run tessera sync TESSERA_LEDGER_URL="postgresql+psycopg://tessera@db/tessera" uv run tessera serve Secrets never go in the file. The only secret Tessera uses, an optional NCBI API key, is read from the environment variable named by [sources.pubmed] api_key_env .

title: Running Tessera
heading: Running Tessera
text: Running Tessera Tessera is one Python application and one folder of data. This guide covers what is in that folder, how to keep data fresh, backups, upgrades, PostgreSQL, and what to check when something goes wrong.

title: Running Tessera
heading: The data home
text: Everything Tessera stores lives in the data home ( [data] home , ./var by default): var/ raw/ the public sources' responses, exactly as received, one folder per run lake/ normalized records in Parquet files, one folder per table ledger.db people, links, decisions, and run history (SQLite; absent with PostgreSQL) derived/ the search index and concept profiles, rebuilt from the lake and ledger logs/ logs, one JSON object per line These parts are not equally precious: The ledger is the only part that holds human work : people, decisions, notes. Back it up. The lake and raw downloads come from public sources and can be fetched again. Keeping raw/ lets tessera replay rebuild the lake without the

title: Running Tessera
heading: Keeping data fresh
text: Run uv run tessera sync on a schedule. After the first sync it fetches only what changed, so a daily run usually takes a few minutes. Each source's expected freshness appears on the Sources page, which warns when a source is overdue or its last run failed. A daily cron entry (Linux or macOS): 30 2 * * * cd /srv/tessera && /usr/local/bin/uv run tessera --quiet sync A systemd timer works the same way: run uv run tessera --quiet sync from the folder that holds tessera.toml , as the user who owns the data home. Send the weekly digest of pending work (each group's inbox, and the review queues) by email once a week, after a sync. It needs a mail server under [mail] (see Configuration ); without on

title: Running Tessera
heading: Serving the app
text: uv run tessera serve Tessera listens on 127.0.0.1:8000 by default ( [server] host and port ).

title: Running Tessera
heading: Accounts and sign-in
text: Out of the box Tessera runs in single-operator mode : no sign-in, answering only on this machine, with every decision recorded under [server] operator . That suits one curator on a laptop. For several people, or for a server others reach, turn on accounts: Create the first admin (you are asked for a password of at least 12 characters): `` bash uv run tessera users add ada --name "Ada Okafor" --role admin `` Set accounts = true under [server] , and host to the address to listen on (for example 0.0.0.0 ). Put Tessera behind HTTPS, typically a reverse proxy such as nginx or Caddy that forwards to it, so that passwords and session cookies travel encrypted. Have the proxy pass the original host (

The search index, discovery files, a

heading: Restoring

heading: The exit export
text: tessera export writes everything Tessera knows in open formats, readable without Tessera, for leaving it or for analysis elsewhere: uv run tessera export /mnt/exports/tessera-2026-11-08 The folder has every ledger table (people, names and identifiers, groups and memberships, every link with its evidence and decision, the decision logs, pages, reports, and settings) and every lake table (the current version of each record fetched from PubMed, iCite, NIH RePORTER, ClinicalTrials.gov, ORCID, and MeSH), each as Parquet and CSV; report snapshots; DATA-DICTIONARY.md , describing every table and column; and a manifest.json with row counts and digests. Password hashes and browser sessions are left o

title: Running Tessera
heading: Operations and alerts
text: Admin → Operations shows, for administrators: Operations what needs attention now: runs that failed or partly failed in the last two days, sources that have gone stale, and a backup older than [alerts] backup_days ; every source and job over the last 30 days: the last run and when it last succeeded, runs, failures, the typical time a run takes and the recent run times, and the last error; the sizes of the ledger, the lake (table by table), the raw responses, the search and discovery files, report snapshots, and backups kept in the data home; the last backup, and whether a data job is running now. The same is at GET /api/v1/operations .

title: Running Tessera
heading: Alerts
text: Set who hears about problems, and give Tessera a mail server (see Configuration ): [alerts] email = ["research-it@example.edu"] backup_days = 7 tessera sync then sends one email at its end when there are issues, and tessera alerts --send does the same at any time ( tessera alerts alone lists them). The same set of issues is sent once, and again after a week if it persists; --force sends it now. A sync never fails because an alert could not be sent.

title: Running Tessera
heading: Upgrading
text: git pull uv sync uv run tessera db upgrade # apply ledger migrations, if any uv run tessera build search # rebuild the index with the new version uv run tessera build discovery # and concept profiles and the graph tessera doctor and the web app's health check ( /api/v1/health ) report a ledger that needs db upgrade . Migrations keep every row: they are tested on SQLite and PostgreSQL with a populated ledger, upgrading and downgrading. Take a backup before upgrading anyway ( tessera backup ). The changelog notes anything that needs more than these steps.

title: Running Tessera
heading: PostgreSQL
text: SQLite suits one organization on one machine well. To keep the ledger in PostgreSQL instead: uv sync --extra postgres Then set [ledger] url = "postgresql+psycopg://tessera@dbhost/tessera" (or TESSERA_LEDGER_URL ) and run uv run tessera db upgrade to create the schema. Put the password in the standard PGPASSWORD variable or a .pgpass file rather than in the URL. The lake and search index stay in the data home either way.

title: Running Tessera
heading: Lake maintenance
text: The lake keeps earlier versions of records when sources update them. Occasionally: uv run tessera lake status # files and rows per table uv run tessera lake compact # rewrite each table to current rows only uv run tessera lake gc # delete superseded files older than 7 days

title: Running Tessera
heading: When something goes wrong
text: tessera doctor checks the configuration, the data home, the ledger schema, and the database engines Tessera relies on (SQLite full-text search and DuckDB); tessera doctor --online also checks that each public source can be reached. tessera runs and the Sources page show failed or partial runs with the source's error. Logs are in <data home>/logs . Add -v to any command for more detail. A source changed or was down: run uv run tessera sync again; completed work is not repeated. Search looks out of date: uv run tessera build search rebuilds it from the lake and ledger in seconds.

title: The assistant
heading: The assistant
text: The assistant Tessera can include an assistant that answers questions from Tessera's own records, citing them. It is optional and off by default : until the configuration turns it on, nothing in the app, the API, or the public site mentions it, and no model is ever called. Everything else in Tessera works the same with it off.

title: The assistant
heading: What it does, and what it never does
text: It answers from the records the person asking may read, through the same access policy as every page. It cannot change anything. It cites the records it used, and declines what the records do not support. Nothing sent to a model includes contact details (email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses) or links nobody has accepted. Every exchange is logged: who asked, when, the provider and model, the prompt's version, the messages and tool calls with the records they returned, the answer, its citations, tokens, and time. Admins read the log in Admin → Assistant . Admin → Assistant

title: The assistant
heading: Asking a question
text: With the assistant on, Ask appears in the top bar (and as Ask a question… in the command palette, ⌘K or Ctrl-K). It opens a side panel. Type a question and press Enter. While the assistant works, the panel shows each step: "Finding who works on …", "Opening …", "Counting …". The answer streams in as it is written, with numbered citations. The records it cites are listed under it; open one to see the record. Ask a follow-up in the same panel and the assistant keeps the conversation. New conversation starts over. Stop ends an answer early. A stopped answer is kept in the log, and its citations are not shown, since they were never checked. Ask It answers questions such as: Who works on a topic,

Each tool asks Tessera's own API, in the same request the person's browser would make, with their session, so it sees exactly what they may see and nothing else. heading: Plain-language summaries
text: With the assistant on, a profile or a group can have a short summary of its work for a general reader: patients, donors, students, journalists. Nobody sees a summary until someone responsible for it approves it. Who reviews: for a profile, the person themselves (when their account is linked to it), a curator for them, or an admin; for a group, its managers and curators. Drafting: a reviewer chooses Draft a summary on the profile, or on the group's page. The facts come from confirmed records only (positions, topics, recent confirmed papers, grants, and studies; for a group, also its published page and its leaders), read with the reviewer's own access, and the model is told to use nothing else

title: The assistant
heading: Turning it on
text: Add an [ai] section to the configuration and restart tessera serve . The starting configuration that tessera init writes (and tessera.example.toml ) ends with one, commented out, listing every setting: remove the # before [ai] and each setting you need. Keys are never written in the file: the configuration names the environment variable that holds one, and a key written in the file stops Tessera from starting. provider is the protocol the endpoint speaks: provider Speaks Works with openai OpenAI's Chat Completions API OpenAI, and any endpoint that speaks it: Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio, gateways anthropic Anthropic's Messages API Anthropic, and any endpoint that speaks it: Ollama, gateways bedro

title: The assistant
heading: Trying it on the demo
text: The demo (see Getting started ) is built with the assistant off. To try it there, add an [ai] section to the end of demo/tessera.toml . This one uses Ollama on the same machine, which needs no key from Tessera; Ollama must be running with the model available, and any of the providers above works the same way: [ai] enabled = true provider = "openai" base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1" model = "gemma4:31b-cloud" Then check the connection and start (or restart) the demo: uv run tessera --config demo/tessera.toml ai check uv run tessera --config demo/tessera.toml serve Ask now appears in the top bar: try "Who works on CAR-T cell therapy?" or "How many papers has the organization published eac

title: The assistant
heading: Choosing a model
text: The assistant relies on the model to call tools and to cite what they return, so a model needs tool calling. Larger models follow the instructions more reliably. Small local models are fine for trying it out; for everyday use, choose a model your organization trusts with the records the assistant reads, since everything it is sent leaves Tessera.

title: Changelog
heading: Evaluation
text: Pilot check against people's own ORCID works lists: Tessera reads an ORCID record only once the iD is confirmed, and none was, so the records behind the 49 suggested iDs are independent of every score. Of 193 papers that 39 people list themselves (within the pilot's two-year window), 95.3% were found as candidates (target 95%); of those, 97.3% are in the strong band and all are at or above the review threshold. Works lists measure recall, not precision: people list only some of their papers. Details are in spec/evidence-engine.md . Learned weights and auto-accept need curator decisions, which the pilot does not have yet. On generated decisions, fitting recovers the weights that produced them

title: Changelog
heading: Fixed
text: On SQLite, a migration that failed part way could leave some of its schema changes behind, because Python's driver did not put them in the transaction. Schema changes are now transactional and roll back whole (a test checks it). A person listed on several roster rows without any identifier became several people; within one file, such rows with the same full name are now one person. Keyboard hints on buttons were faded below WCAG AA contrast; they are now full strength. Resolving again rewrote hundreds of unchanged suggestions because tied topics were listed in a random order in their explanations; ties are now broken by name, and a second resolve changes nothing.

title: Changelog
text: The first release. Tessera builds an organization's research graph from public data, with the evidence for every link, and gives curators fast tools to confirm it. It runs on a laptop or a single server. Highlights: connectors for PubMed, iCite, NIH RePORTER, and ClinicalTrials.gov; a people directory from grant investigators, an optional roster, and discovered authors; explainable authorship suggestions; links between papers, grants, and studies; a fast, accessible web app in three palettes with light and dark versions; a keyboard-driven review queue; a JSON API; and user guides.

title: Changelog
heading: Evaluation
text: Pilot check against ORCID iDs at a mid-sized research institute (70 directory members, about 2,400 publications over five years; 588 matched papers labeled by the ORCID iD printed on them): the strong band was 98.3% precise at 93.7% recall (target 99%), and suggestions above the review threshold were 97.9% precise at 95.8% recall (target 90%). Seven of the nine strong-band disagreements appear to be people with a second ORCID iD rather than wrong matches. Details are in spec/evidence-engine.md .
